I think it is an awesome movie with a few great set pieces. I think it is a mistake to make it about anything more than a tale of a troubled man's descent into madness, though. It is less a social commentary than a psychological one.

It starts by masking D-FENS's true identity. He goes from sympathetic character to loathesome one, hero to villain slowly in the space of two hours. It is a good piece of storytelling.

He starts with abandonning his car in rush hour. Who hasn't wanted to do that? We applaud the chutzpa. Then he goes off on a shop owner who seems to be acting unreasonably. That said, this is the first inkling he may not really be a good guy, though. His actions are out of proportion to his predicament (this is consistent with things we learn later such as that his marriage fell apart because he is violent).

The next few actions show him defeating characters which are stock bad guys from central casting (gangbangers and nazis) and are supposed to put him in a good light. We should maybe be thinking he is a sympathetic vigilante like Charles Bronson in Death Wish. That story is falling apart, though, as we also watch the other story with Robert Duvall.

Robert Duvall plays a character who is a mirror of Michael Douglas. Both have had disappointments, mundane careers, family problems. But whereas Michael Douglas's character appears strong but is actually taking a weak course (rather than get his act together he intends a murder suicide with his kid), Duvall is the opposite. He appears weak with the back story of his wife, but he has an actual quiet strength.

It is a movie about how man reacts to hardship and contrasts a flawed hero with a villain who sees himself as a victim. His victim staus is partly a commentary on modern society and how it estranges man from his environment but it is mostly just a personal commentary on personal weakness in the face of adversity.
